To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rigidity of the network is the main determinant of the thermal reversibility of the glass transition and that the fragility of glass-forming melts is a direct consequence of the enthalpic change at the glass transition, which in turn is controlled by the network rigidity.
the glass transition is reversible for isostatically rigid systems (with no enthalpic changes), whereas it is irreversible for systems that are too soft (with large enthalpic changes).

(1) a low temperature dynamics of a Keatin-like model shows that a glass with minimal enthalpy change is formed when the system is isostatically constrained, (2) the isostatically constrained glass is a strong (Arrheniuis-like) glass-former, (3) these findings are confirmed by experimental studies of chalcogenide glasses, and (4) the approach fails for weakly interacting systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of rigidity in network glasses, and the connection between rigidity and glass transition.
the relationship between the structural rigidity of network glasses, the reversibility of the glass transition and their fragility.

the study of the glass transition and of the strong–fragility behaviour of glass-formers from the viewpoint of network rigidity and its relationship with the thermal reversibility of the glass transition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the isostatic condition is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the formation of strong (fragile) network glasses.
isostatically rigidity is a sufficient condition for a strong glass-forming liquid and for a reversible glass transition.
a strong glass-forming liquid is a system which is isostatically constrained and has a reversible glass transition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the glass transition of network glasses can be understood as a transition between two states of the same system with different rigidity.
a strong glass-forming liquid is obtained when the glass-former is optimally constrained during the cooling process.
the rigidity of glasses is a key parameter for understanding the glass transition and its relationship with the fragility of glass-forming melts.
The main takeaway from our work is that

rigidity is a key concept in the understanding of the nature of glass-forming systems and that the glass transition is a reversible phenomenon when the glass is isostatically constrained, i.e. in the absence of any thermal or structural relaxation.
the glass transition is a thermally reversible phenomenon, and that it is the nature of the glass network that controls the reversibility.
the nature of glass formation is strongly related to the nature of the network rigidity.
